sentences.text: Her grandmother had thirteen creels in the water off the point, and had had them there for forty years, and in April she had a stroke.
It was a small one, as those things go.
She came home after nine days and she could walk with a stick and she was extremely irritated about the stick.
But her hands did not do what she asked them to any more, and there was no version of the situation in which she was going out to the point in a punt.
So Maeve went.

She was eleven, which everyone had opinions about, and the arrangement was that she went with her father when he was in and with Mr Nolan when he was not, and that she never, under any circumstances, went alone.
She hauled thirteen creels twice a week from April to July.
It was heavier than she had understood.
That was the thing that surprised her — not the cold and not the early mornings, which she had been warned about, but the sheer physical arithmetic of a creel full of water coming up over a gunwale.
She got better at it.
She got a system.
She got a place on her right palm that stopped being a blister and started being something else.
The system was this.
You came at the creel from downtide, so the punt held still against the rope instead of swinging off it.
You took the buoy with the hook and never with your hand, because your hand would be wet and cold and would not close properly by the fourth one.

You brought the creel up in three pulls with a rest between, and on the rest you put your forearm along the gunwale and let the wood take the weight instead of your back — which her grandmother had taught her without a single word, by putting one hand on her shoulder and pressing down until Maeve moved her arm to the right place herself.
And you did not look into the creel until it was aboard.
That was the important one.
Looking early made you hurry, and hurrying was how a rope went over the side, and a rope over the side in April water was how a girl of eleven became a thing that happened in that bay.
Thirteen creels took about two and a half hours with Mr Nolan, who talked the entire time about a dispute over a mooring that had begun in 1998.
It took about ninety minutes with her father, who did not talk at all, and who watched her do the third pull on every single creel without ever once offering to take it.
Her grandmother asked about them every evening, in the same words, from the chair by the window.

*What were they like.* And Maeve would go through them in order — this one heavy, this one empty, weed on the north two, a crab in the fifth that was undersized and went back — and her grandmother would listen with her eyes shut and say *mm* in the places where *mm* went.
Sometimes she would say *that's the ground there* or *she'll fill next week*, and once she said *your grandfather lost that one twice*, about a creel that was in fact new.

That quarter of an hour was the part of the day that Maeve did not mind at all, and she understood at the time that she was going to remember it, which almost never happens while a thing is still going on.
And in the second week of July she decided she was going to stop.
She decided it on a Tuesday, rowing back in, with an empty box and a low sky and her hands hurting in a new way.
It was not dramatic.
She was not crying.

She had simply run the numbers, the way you do at eleven when nobody is watching, and the numbers said: her grandmother was not going to be able to do this again, and her father could not do this and his own boat, and Mr Nolan was seventy-one, and she could not do it alone for the rest of her life, and every week she kept it going was a week that made the ending harder for everybody.
The kindest thing, she thought, was to stop now while it was still her doing it.
She was going to say it that evening at the table.
She had the sentence ready.
She had been building it since the point.
She rowed in past the black buoy with the sentence in her mouth.
